elements.text: Why Bridges Don't All Look the Same

shots.narration: So why don't bridges all look the same? It isn't because one design is simply better than the others. Each form is a different answer to the same problem, shaped by materials, by the site, by the span, and by the time it was built in.
shots.visual_purpose: Title card: the central question [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (7 elements)]

items.text: 2 · The problem every bridge must solve

elements.text: 2 · The problem every bridge must solve

shots.narration: Every bridge has the same basic job. It has to carry loads: the traffic crossing it, and the weight of the bridge itself. And it has to pass all of that down through its supports into the ground.
shots.visual_purpose: A whole bridge; the load on its deck and the ground it must reach [HOLD 1/1: hold steel_truss_bridge]

elements.text: Conceptual load path — not to scale

shots.narration: Engineers often describe a bridge in two parts. The superstructure is the part that spans the gap, including the deck. The substructure is what holds it up: abutments at the ends, and sometimes piers in between. Load follows a path from the deck, through both parts, into the foundations.
shots.visual_purpose: Superstructure over substructure; a conceptual path to the foundations [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold steel_truss_bridge, glowing substructure from sentence 2]

shots.narration: What changes from one bridge to the next is how that path is arranged. So let's start again with an empty gap.
shots.visual_purpose: The empty site: the gap any structure must span [SITE_HOLD 1/1: the empty shared site: the gap any of the structures must span]

shots.narration: The first answer is the beam. Lay a strong member across the gap, support it at each end, and you have a bridge. It is one of the oldest ideas in bridge building.
shots.visual_purpose: A timber beam bridge appears on the empty site [ASSEMBLE_IN 1/2: timber_beam_bridge assembles into the shown empty site (its parts drop in by assembly layer)]

shots.narration: This timber bridge is a row of short beam spans. Planks form the deck, long beams carry the planks, cap beams carry the beams, and posts carry the caps.

shots.narration: Each beam carries its load by resisting bending. At each support, a cap beam spreads the load onto the posts. The posts then carry it down into the ground in compression.
shots.visual_purpose: Beam, cap, posts: the path to the ground [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold timber_beam_bridge, glowing stringer from sentence 0]

shots.narration: Beams are simple, and wood was usually easy to find. That is why timber beam bridges were still being built long after timber trusses stopped being competitive, and in 2005 a national report found them still being built on quiet rural roads and in parks. But many early timber bridges had relatively short spans, which is why this one needs so many posts.
shots.visual_purpose: The posts that short spans require [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold timber_beam_bridge, glowing trestle_bent from sentence 2; slow push-in (12%)]

shots.narration: A masonry arch takes a different approach. It is built from wedge-shaped stones called voussoirs, with a keystone at the crown.
shots.visual_purpose: One arch ring's voussoirs and keystone read as separate wedge-shaped pieces [CLOSEUP_EXPLODE 1/2: establish stone_arch_bridge with arch_ring glowing]

shots.narration: The curve turns the downward load into thrust along the arch, pressing the stones together. So the arch works mainly in compression. At each end it pushes outward and down on its supports, and the supports push back.
shots.visual_purpose: Thrust along one ring; inclined reactions [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold stone_arch_bridge, glowing arch_ring from sentence 0]

shots.narration: That is why arches suit materials that are strong under compression, like stone. And it is why the supports matter so much: the abutments have to push inward on the arch, against its thrust.
shots.visual_purpose: The supports that hold the arch's ends [HOLD 1/1: hold stone_arch_bridge]

shots.narration: Building an arch takes support of its own. While a stone arch is being built, a temporary timber frame called falsework holds the stones in place. So building one called for carpenters as well as skilled masons.
shots.visual_purpose: Falsework under an arch ring (diagram) [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (30 elements)]

elements.text: Lower cost made up for less permanence

shots.narration: Stone arches were generally more expensive to build than timber bridges. But stone was the preferred choice where durability and permanence were required, so arches were favoured on busy routes and in important places. Elsewhere, the lower cost of timber made up for its lack of permanence.
shots.visual_purpose: Cost versus permanence panel [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (15 elements)]

elements.text: Conceptual load path — not to scale

shots.narration: A third approach is the truss. It builds a structure out of straight members, joined into triangles. Each member is mainly pulled or pushed along its length, in tension or in compression.
shots.visual_purpose: Triangulated members and joints [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold steel_truss_bridge, glowing truss_members from sentence 1]

elements.text: Conceptual load path — not to scale

shots.narration: In a simple span like these, under a downward load, the top chord is squeezed and the bottom chord is stretched. Inside, some web members are in compression and others are in tension.
shots.visual_purpose: Chords named, web members not colour-coded [HOLD 1/1: hold steel_truss_bridge]

shots.narration: The triangles can be arranged in different patterns. This is a Pratt truss. In the original design, patented in 1844, its verticals were timber and its diagonals were iron rods. Swap the web for diagonals that alternate in direction, and you have a Warren truss, patented in 1848. Both patterns carry load through triangles; they simply arrange the members differently.

shots.narration: Trusses also changed how bridges were built. By the middle of the nineteenth century, shops were making and drilling truss members, then shipping them to the bridge site, ready to assemble. And by 1860, the railroads relied almost entirely on these prefabricated parts.

elements.text: A wider crossing (illustrative, not to scale)

shots.narration: To cross wide rivers and deep gorges, bridges needed longer spans. Wide rivers like the Ohio and the Mississippi, and deep gorges like the one at Niagara, needed bridges that could reach farther.
shots.visual_purpose: The wide crossing, empty [SITE_HOLD 1/1: the empty shared site: the gap any of the structures must span]

shots.narration: One answer was the cantilever. Hold your arm straight out from your shoulder, and it is acting as a cantilever: supported at one end, free at the other, like a diving board.
shots.visual_purpose: A cantilever truss assembles on the wide crossing [ASSEMBLE_IN 1/1: cantilever_bridge assembles into the shown empty site (its parts drop in by assembly layer)]

shots.narration: A cantilever bridge is a modified beam. Anchor arms rest on the banks and the main piers, cantilever arms reach out over the river, and a suspended span hangs between their tips.
shots.visual_purpose: Anchor arms, cantilever arms and the suspended span [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold cantilever_bridge, glowing cantilever_truss from sentence 1]

items.text: Built outward: no falsework in the channel

elements.text: Built outward: no falsework in the channel

shots.narration: Its great advantage came during construction. The arms could be built outward from the piers with no falsework blocking the channel below, and then the suspended span was lifted into place.
shots.visual_purpose: The suspended span lifts out of the arms and returns [EXPLODE 1/1: take cantilever_bridge apart by assembly layer (14 components, 4 layers) and back; 2 focus components glow]

elements.text: Photo: Jet Lowe, HAER, Library of Congress (public domain)

shots.narration: In the United States, cantilevers were a standard answer for intermediate to longer spans from the 1880s to the 1960s. The Queensboro Bridge in New York was the country's longest cantilever when it was completed in 1909. Unlike our model, it has no suspended span in the middle, something one report calls unique among cantilevers of its size.
shots.visual_purpose: Archival photograph of the Queensboro Bridge [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (10 elements)]

shots.narration: For the longest spans of all, engineers hung the deck instead. In a suspension bridge, the deck hangs from vertical suspenders attached to great main cables.
shots.visual_purpose: The deck hanging from the cables [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold suspension_bridge, glowing hanger from sentence 1]

elements.text: Conceptual load path — not to scale

shots.narration: The cables are in tension, and they pass over towers that are in compression. At each end, the cables are anchored, usually in large masses of stone or concrete.
shots.visual_purpose: Cables in tension, towers in compression, the anchorages [HOLD 1/1: hold suspension_bridge]

shots.narration: A suspension deck is light for its span, and it can be very flexible. So a stiffening truss is commonly built under the deck, against wind and earthquakes.
shots.visual_purpose: The stiffening truss under the deck [HIGHLIGHT_THEN_EXPLODE 1/2: glow stiffening_truss]

shots.narration: A suspension deck is light for its span, and it can be very flexible. So a stiffening truss is commonly built under the deck, against wind and earthquakes.
shots.visual_purpose: The stiffening truss under the deck [HIGHLIGHT_THEN_EXPLODE 2/2: take suspension_bridge apart by assembly layer (8 components, 4 layers) and back; 2 focus components glow]

elements.text: Photo: HAER, Library of Congress (public domain)

shots.narration: The Brooklyn Bridge in New York, completed in 1883, was planned with two towers, cables and suspenders, anchorages and a stiffening truss. One report says few suspension bridges built since can claim to stand entirely clear of its shadow.
shots.visual_purpose: Archival photograph of the Brooklyn Bridge [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (8 elements)]

shots.narration: A cable-stayed bridge also relies on steel cables, but it uses them differently. Straight stay cables run from tall towers directly down to the edges of the deck.
shots.visual_purpose: Stays running from the towers to the deck edges [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold cable_stayed_bridge, glowing stay_cable from sentence 1]

elements.text: Suspension: shorter towers, main cables to anchorages
Cable-stayed: taller towers, stays end at the deck

shots.narration: Drawn in outline at the same span, the two types differ. The suspension bridge has much shorter towers, and its main cables run over them to anchorages at each end. The cable-stayed bridge needs taller towers, because their height depends on the span, and its stays end at the deck itself.
shots.visual_purpose: Suspension and cable-stayed elevations compared (diagram) [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (71 elements)]

elements.text: Conceptual load path — not to scale

shots.narration: Once the towers are up, the deck can be built outward from them in both directions, without falsework towers, until the spans meet. The stays also squeeze the deck along its length, and that squeeze builds up toward the towers.
shots.visual_purpose: The deck segments return outward from the towers [EXPLODE 1/1: take cable_stayed_bridge apart by assembly layer (41 components, 6 layers) and back; 21 focus components glow]

elements.text: Where long spans pay off (United States)
Suspension by 2012: as spans approach 3,000 ft
After FHWA, Steel Bridge Design Handbook (FHWA-IF-12-052), 2012

shots.narration: Before 1970, suspension bridges were thought to be the cheapest way to span more than about 1,200 feet. By 2012, a federal handbook said cable-stayed bridges become very competitive above 750 feet, and that suspension bridges pay off only as main spans approach 3,000.
shots.visual_purpose: Span economics (sourced values only) [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (17 elements)]

shots.narration: So which design is best? The honest answer is that it depends. Materials, the site, the span, cost, and the skills available all pull in different directions.
shots.visual_purpose: The factors that shape a bridge [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (8 elements)]

shots.narration: Start with the materials themselves. An arch needs a material that is strong under compression, and stone is.
shots.visual_purpose: Stone in compression: the arch rings [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold stone_arch_bridge, glowing arch_ring from sentence 1]

items.text: Wrought iron: valued in tension and compression

elements.text: Wrought iron: valued in tension and compression

shots.narration: A truss needs members that can work in tension as well as compression. Wrought iron was valued for exactly that: one historian calls it a material strong equally in tension and in compression.
shots.visual_purpose: Truss members that work both ways [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold steel_truss_bridge, glowing truss_members from sentence 0]

items.text: Timber: plentiful and cheap, but it decays

elements.text: Timber: plentiful and cheap, but it decays

shots.narration: Wood was often plentiful and cheap, but wooden bridges were vulnerable to decay.
shots.visual_purpose: The timber structure [HOLD 1/1: hold timber_beam_bridge]

elements.text: Photo: Jack E. Boucher, HAER, Library of Congress (public domain)

shots.narration: That is one reason many timber truss bridges were covered with a roof and siding, to protect them from the weather. This is the Humpback Covered Bridge, built in 1857 over Dunlap Creek.
shots.visual_purpose: Archival photograph of a covered timber bridge [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (8 elements)]

items.text: Iron chains: only as strong as the weakest link

elements.text: Iron chains: only as strong as the weakest link

shots.narration: Cables have a materials story of their own. America's first metal suspension bridges hung from iron chains, and many failed after only a few years: critics said such a bridge was only as good as the weakest link in one of its chains. Wire cables answered that fear, and suspension and cable-stayed bridges came to rely on high-strength steel cables.
shots.visual_purpose: The main cables of the suspension model [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold suspension_bridge, glowing main_cable from sentence 2]

elements.text: Down and up again: too steep for trains
A viaduct keeps the line nearly level

shots.narration: The site of a bridge matters too. Railway engines have limited traction, so railways need gentle gradients. Where a valley was too deep and wide to fill with an embankment, engineers built viaducts and trestles to keep the line nearly straight and level.
shots.visual_purpose: Valley profile with a level line on piers [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (11 elements)]

elements.text: Suspension: cables anchored in massive blocks or in bedrock
Cable-stayed: good rock near the surface is not required

shots.narration: Long spans make the ground beneath them matter even more. A suspension bridge has to anchor its cables in massive blocks, or directly in bedrock. The towers of a cable-stayed bridge, by contrast, can be built where good rock does not lie near the surface.
shots.visual_purpose: Ground and foundations for the two cable families (schematic) [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (40 elements)]

items.text: Hinged: superstructure could adjust if a pier sank

elements.text: Hinged: superstructure could adjust if a pier sank

shots.narration: A cantilever like this one is a continuous girder with hinges built in, which made its forces easy to calculate. So on unstable soil, if a pier sank, its superstructure could adjust, where a continuous beam might build up hidden stresses and fail.
shots.visual_purpose: The cantilever's main piers [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold cantilever_bridge, glowing pier from sentence 1]

items.text: Tacoma Narrows, 1940: lost to the wind

elements.text: Tacoma Narrows, 1940: lost to the wind

shots.narration: Then there is the wind. In 1940, the four-month-old Tacoma Narrows suspension bridge collapsed in only moderately high winds. The disaster led to intense research on wind, and later suspension bridges were built to new standards for stiffened decks.
shots.visual_purpose: The stiffening truss under the suspension deck (no collapse is shown) [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold suspension_bridge, glowing stiffening_truss from sentence 2]

elements.text: Two kinds of span numbers (steel bridge handbook, 2012)
Plate girder: about 90 to over 500 ft
Simple truss: about 450 to about 750 ft
Suspension: economic as main spans approach 3,000 ft
After FHWA, Steel Bridge Design Handbook (FHWA-IF-12-052), 2012 — ranges, not limits of what a type can span

shots.narration: Span decides a great deal. A 2012 federal handbook for steel bridges gives two kinds of numbers. Some are practical ranges: plate girders from about 90 to over 500 feet, simple trusses from about 450 to about 750, and cantilever trusses considerably farther. Others are spans that have actually been built: arches from about 200 to 1,800 feet, and cable-stayed bridges from under 200 to nearly 3,000. And as we saw, suspension bridges only pay off as main spans approach 3,000 feet.
shots.visual_purpose: Practical ranges and built spans of the six families, kept apart (sourced values only) [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (30 elements)]

shots.narration: Cost and skill pull in different directions. A cantilever avoided the expensive anchorages a suspension bridge needs. And a suspension bridge often takes a long time to build: installing its main cables calls for expertise that very few contractors have.
shots.visual_purpose: The anchorages and main cables of the suspension model [HOLD_HIGHLIGHT 1/1: hold suspension_bridge, glowing anchorage from sentence 1]

shots.narration: By 2012, cable-stayed bridges were becoming more common worldwide, and one significant reason was that the methods for erecting them had become better understood.
shots.visual_purpose: The cable-stayed model [HOLD 1/1: hold cable_stayed_bridge; slow push-in (10%)]

elements.text: Metal trusses spread; stone arches decline

shots.narration: Finally, every bridge belongs to its time. As metal trusses spread, skilled masons became fewer and reinforced concrete arrived, stone arch construction declined. Then, during the Great Depression, it briefly returned.
shots.visual_purpose: Timeline (dates from the evidence registry) [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (31 elements)]

elements.text: 1980–2012: almost all new U.S. bridges with
main spans over 1,000 ft were cable-stayed
Long spans: a timeline of their own

shots.narration: Long spans have a timeline of their own. By 1849, a suspension bridge at Wheeling spanned 1,010 feet, the longest span in the world when it opened. Cantilevers were a standard American answer from the 1880s to the 1960s, and a 2012 federal handbook found that almost every American bridge built since 1980 with a main span over 1,000 feet was cable-stayed.

elements.text: United States — schematic, not to scale

shots.narration: These trade-offs played out across nineteenth-century America as the railways spread. In the East, railroads built massive stone viaducts, while western builders generally used timber. Three documented examples show how differently builders answered.
shots.visual_purpose: Schematic map: East and West [CARD 1/1: 2D card supplied by the beat (15 elements)]

shots.narration: Near Baltimore, the Carrollton Viaduct was completed in 1829. Built of roughly twelve thousand granite blocks, it carries the railway over Gwynns Falls on an eighty foot arch. A national report in 2005 called it the world's oldest stone railroad span still in service.

shots.narration: Early railroads needed durable bridges to carry heavy trains. For a line meant to last, stone was the answer.

shots.narration: In the West, the pressure was different. Railroads had to open new lines quickly and economically, and timber was abundant and cheap. This timber trestle near Corinne, Utah, was built in 1872 by the Central Pacific Railroad.

shots.narration: Iron offered a third path. The Bollman truss, patented in 1852, was one of the first designs to use iron in all of its essential structural parts. It could be built relatively quickly and inexpensively, while offering the long-lasting qualities of metal. The bridge at Savage, Maryland, is the only remaining example of the design.

shots.narration: Long spans forced hard decisions too. In 1855, John Roebling's suspension bridge carried trains across the Niagara Gorge, but railroad executives doubted that suspension bridges could bear heavy trains. Their doubts were not unjustified: the bridge needed substantial repairs in 1877 and 1880, and it was declared inadequate in 1890.

shots.narration: In America, modern cantilevers were first used by the railroads, and only later for highways. A cantilever is inherently rigid, so if properly designed, heavy locomotives pulling trains are no threat to it. In 1877, one carried the Cincinnati Southern Railroad across the 275-foot-deep Kentucky River gorge: the longest cantilever in the world.

shots.narration: In Maine, a modern cable-stayed bridge went up remarkably fast. The Penobscot Narrows Bridge, opened in 2006, carries its 1,161-foot main span on two concrete pylons 430 feet tall. It took just 42 months from conception to completion, and one of its pylons has a public observatory at the top.

shots.narration: So why don't bridges all look the same? Because a bridge's form comes from two things working together. One is how its structure carries load: beams resist bending, arches work in compression, and trusses share load among members in tension and compression.

elements.text: 2 · The world it was built in

shots.narration: The other is the world it was built in: its materials, its site, its span, its budget and its builders.

elements.text: is the plate girder, a beam
simple and easy to put up

shots.narration: And it is not a simple story of progress. Timber beam bridges were still being built long after timber trusses stopped being competitive, and stone arches briefly returned during the Great Depression. And in 2012, a federal handbook still named a kind of beam, the welded plate girder, as the most common steel bridge. At one time, a great number of small suspension bridges were built across the country, simply because they were easy to put up. Each form can still be the right answer in the right place.
